book: Nala and Damayanti (from Indian Idylls / Hindu Literature)

chunks.why: Introduction and idyll: Nala the ideal prince and Damayanti the peerless princess fall in love by swan-messenger.
Gods intercept Nala en route to Swayamvara and force him to plead their suit; Damayanti secretly vows only he.
Damayanti chooses Nala over the gods; wedding, boons, prosperous rule, children born, Aswamedha performed.
Kali possesses Nala; he gambles away kingdom, gold, robes to Pushkara; Damayanti sends children to safety.
Stripped, exiled, starving; townsfolk forbidden to help; birds steal his last cloth; Nala abandons sleeping Damayanti.
Damayanti wakes alone, seized by a python, saved by a hunter who then tries to rape her; she curses him dead.
She wanders begging tigers and mountains for news; hermits comfort her with prophecy of reunion, then vanish.
Joins a caravan; rogue elephants stampede the camp at night, trampling merchants; she wakes to carnage.
Survivors blame Damayanti as demon-witch; she flees, reaches Chedi city, taken in as handmaid to the queen-mother.
Snake Karkotaka's bite disguises Nala as dwarf Vahuka, serving Rituparna as charioteer; Sudeva spots Damayanti.
Sudeva identifies Damayanti by her mole; she returns to father Bhima, reunited with children and kin.
Parnada finds Nala's coded reply at Rituparna's court; Damayanti sets fake second Swayamvara as bait; Nala harnesses horses.
Nala trades horse-lore for numbers-skill; Kali is expelled from him, cursed into a tree; freed, he speeds to Vidarbha.
In Vidarbha, Keshini tests Vahuka; he weeps at coded verse and performs miracles (fire, water, blossoming leaves) that betray him.
Damayanti recognizes him by his cookery, hugs children; Vayu attests her fidelity; Nala dons magic cloth and resumes his form; re-wed by Bhima.
Nala challenges Pushkara at dice, wins back the whole kingdom, spares his brother, returns in triumph to rule Nishadha.
